title: Practitioner Panel Teardown of Anthropic's Claude Legal Plugins — NDA Triage, Skill Evaluation and the Per-Seat Question
pub: Legal Innovation Spotlight (YouTube), hosted by Ted Theodoropoulos
author: Ted Theodoropoulos · Rob Saccone · Josh Kubicki

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: The source accepts that agentic model products create material pressure on legal and other per-seat software businesses, while reinforcing the synthesis’s caution that market turbulence does not prove direct software displacement. It materially extends the cluster by proposing a specific indirect mechanism: agents may reduce software-using headcount and therefore seat demand, even when the underlying software remains in use.
qs: The way he  framed it up is if you can have 10 AI agents do the work of a hundred employees, you don't need a 100 Salesforce seats anymore.
It kills the headcount that uses the software and that kills the per seat revenue model and that could potentially kill the business.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The panel accepts selective, human-led deployment and adds concrete practitioner evidence from NDA triage: agentic workflows can provide useful first-pass issue spotting, but repeated outputs vary and miss legal nuance. It materially develops the cluster by showing how encoded playbooks, prompt design, systematic evaluation and confidentiality controls can operationalise safe workflow redesign.
qs: I would argue that everyone should write down playbooks if they want to scale their knowledge beyond themselves.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s restrained account of legal plugins as encoded procedural playbooks rather than proof of autonomous practice or validated performance. It also reinforces the qualification that encoding legal expertise reproduces a longstanding knowledge-management problem concerning whose judgment is captured and how.
qs: Anthropic took the time to write down a set of skills, prompts, but think of them as playbooks.
Like now that touches variation in expertise and how you encode it and it's been a classic knowledge management challenge for decades, right?

kp.k: Agent-driven headcount reductions could undermine per-seat software pricing
kp.d: Host Ted Theodoropoulos endorses an analysis he encountered on X: agents could reduce the number of employees needing software subscriptions, indirectly threatening vendors' per-seat revenues. His hypothetical substitutes 10 agents for 100 employees; it is a proposed explanation for market turbulence, not demonstrated employment displacement. He expects business-model adjustments rather than treating software's disappearance as inevitable.
qs: if you can have 10 AI agents do the work of a hundred employees, you don't need a 100 Salesforce seats anymore.
So AI doesn't kill the software directly. It kills the headcount that uses the software and that kills the per seat revenue model and that could potentially kill the business.

kp.k: Legal plugins package expertise into executable, reusable playbooks
kp.d: The panel describes Anthropic's legal plugin as written instructions rather than new infrastructure. Rob Saccone explains that combining these playbooks with connectors, document access and a capable model enables repeatable workflows. He frames capturing expertise in this form as a longstanding knowledge-management challenge, while stressing that lawyers and business users can create their own skills.
qs: Plugins are a set of predefined instructions that tell or instruct the model um how to think about a task, how to think about a problem.
But think of these as bundles of mini playbooks, right?
I would argue that everyone should write down playbooks if they want to scale their knowledge beyond themselves.

kp.k: Agentic workflow improves delivery more than demonstrated substantive analysis
kp.d: In Saccone's demonstration, a fabricated NDA labelled mutual but deliberately one-sided received substantively similar criticism from ordinary Claude chat and the legal-plugin workflow. Co-work's distinction was its multi-step execution, file access and formatted Word deliverable: it selected skills, created a task list, screened provisions and generated a triage report. This is a demonstration on a constructed example, not evidence of general equivalence across legal tasks.
qs: it's intentionally written as a very one-sided, very lopsided agreement.
It creates a to-do list.
substantively it was the same and that's what I mean by it's not very different
it makes the overall user experience, the overall process much, much cleaner.

kp.k: NDA triage requires context and human review
kp.d: Josh Kubicki regards the plugin as useful first-pass issue spotting, comparable to a good first-year associate or law student, rather than final legal work. He recommends contextual prompts and custom instructions reflecting practice-specific concerns, such as intellectual-property transfers. His comparison concerns capability and supervision, not measured replacement of junior lawyers.
qs: No one's advocating use this plugin asis and you never have to review an NDA again. Absolutely not true,
think of this as a good first year associate or even a good law student who's really good at issue spotting but doesn't know how to interpret context because NDAs don't live in a vacuum.
it's a decent start, but not reliable as final work product.

kp.k: Unreviewed NDAs represent a proposed market expansion opportunity
kp.d: Saccone estimates 15–20 million NDAs annually and supposes 20–25% receive review, describing the remainder as exposure for non-experts. He references six million US employer businesses and employment agreements in reasoning toward these figures, explicitly presenting them as guesses and assumptions. His argument is that inexpensive AI checks could address work often signed without legal review, not simply replace existing lawyer-reviewed work.
qs: My best guess would be there's probably 15 20 million NDAs.
let's assume maybe 20 25% of those NDAs are actually reviewed by somebody leaving 80% open to risk that a non-legal expert would be like.
So that's the market moving here. It's not that somebody wrote down a playbook.

kp.k: Business playbooks support selective escalation to outside counsel
kp.d: Theodoropoulos describes Infodash's existing approach to software-licence negotiations: after repeated lawyer-guided negotiations, the business handles minor changes internally but escalates unusual or substantive changes. He uses this experience to illustrate how a playbook can encode flexibility and non-negotiable terms, particularly IP ownership. This is a business-process example motivating AI configuration, not a measured AI-driven reduction in legal spending.
qs: if there are just slight modifications, I don't engage my law firm.
But when we get thrown a real curveball, we absolutely pull in our outside counsel.
that's kind of the basis for what a playbook would look like is you kind of talk about where you have flexibility.

kp.k: Exploratory testing finds model–instruction interactions matter
kp.d: Saccone built Skill Check to compare publicly available NDA skills, including a law firm's published checklist, across models using planted issues and his own rubric. He reports that a minimal prompt ranked second among skills and that Gemini 3 Pro scores ranged from 69% to 87%, with concrete checklists outperforming verbose instructions. These are exploratory results from his custom setup; he acknowledges being a non-lawyer and invites review of the rubric rather than claiming validated legal accuracy.
qs: the scores you're seeing are based on a rubric I wrote to judge the output the to judge the response of skill model combination. Did it find the issues that I planted in that NDA?
It's very interesting that prompt only scored number two on the list of skills.
look at the spread of scores from 69% up to 87%.
the more verbose you got, the worse it did.

kp.k: Repeated runs vary; evaluation becomes a professional capability
kp.d: Kubicki reports running the same Co-work command on the same NDA at least 10 times in fresh sessions without memory and observing variability. He recommends learning how particular models respond to different instruction styles and evaluating skills as they are updated. His expectation that multi-model interfaces and local models will become normal within 12–18 months is a forecast, not an observed adoption rate.
qs: I've ran co-work the exact same command prompt on the exact same NDA that we're talking about here at least 10 times
There is variability, right? There just is.
So starting to understand how to evaluate your skill. If you write a skill, how do you evaluate it? Updating that skill and then evaluating models.
what Rob's showing you is at the tip of the iceberg of where a lot of people are going to be in 12 to 18 months.

kp.k: Open rubrics are essential to trusting automated evaluation
kp.d: Saccone discloses that Skill Check uses an LLM to judge outputs against a rubric and known planted issues, not deterministic matching or independent lawyer scoring. He advocates open evaluations and rubrics, and proposes further experimentation with judges comparing other judges' results for convergence and divergence. These are evaluation methods and proposals, not demonstrated substitutes for human verification before legal reliance.
qs: I'm using an um an LLM as judge approach here
It's not a deterministic way of doing it.
I think these evaluations and benchmarks need to be open.
any vendor shipping a benchmark but they don't share you the rubric share with you the rubric like you don't trust it

kp.k: Low experiment costs motivate displacement predictions
kp.d: Saccone reports that approximately 50–60 experiments cost him two dollars. He contrasts this with lawyer rates of $500 or $1,000 per hour and views further automated judging as economically attractive to business owners. His conclusion that displacement is coming is explicitly his opinion; the comparison does not establish equivalence between experiment outputs and completed professional legal services.
qs: it's like 50 60 like experiments here it cost me two bucks
compared to 500 or a,000 bucks an hour.
this is a displacement and it's clearly coming like in in my humble opinion.

kp.k: Issue spotting succeeds while indemnification nuance remains inconsistent
kp.d: Kubicki's qualitative review finds that the example's non-solicitation provision was consistently flagged across his runs. However, he says outputs missed the negligence-versus-gross-negligence distinction in indemnification: his versions focused on lack of reciprocity, while Saccone's grouped the issue under unusual provisions. He regards this as useful first-pass work with important limitations and cautions that human lawyers can also miss such issues.
qs: That nonsolicitation always comes up as a fail, right?
it doesn't call out the difference between negligence and gross negligence.
On Rob's, it doesn't even actually call out indemnification. It just categorizes it on unusual provisions, right?
We can't hold it to the perfect lawyer standard, right? This is a really good first pass.

kp.k: Local files do not guarantee confidentiality or local inference
kp.d: The panel warns that Co-work's access to files on a user's computer does not make processing air-gapped: document content is sent to Anthropic's backend. Saccone distinguishes sandboxing code execution from protecting information under service terms. Participants acknowledge uncertainty about retention and specific contractual protections, recommend reading applicable terms, and warn against sending sensitive documents through free accounts. Saccone additionally reports that most large firms he works with route model traffic through Microsoft relationships and contracts.
qs: the documents, they live on your machine, but they send the content of the document back up to the mother ship at Anthropic
The sandbox doesn't actually change that,
Files that you're giving access to co-work just because they appear on your laptop and they are right there is they're they're not airgapped, right?
You have to read the terms of service if you're going to use it for serious stuff.

kp.k: Purpose-built legal software can add value beyond underlying models
kp.d: Saccone argues that enterprise legal-AI systems can add connections, context management, memory, legal workflows and output checks that do not come with a raw model. He rejects treating all such products as thin wrappers, while emphasizing buyers' difficulty distinguishing offerings and the need to assess utility. He explicitly says he has never used Harvey, qualifying his favorable characterization as indirect judgment rather than firsthand product evaluation.
qs: it's not from direct knowledge just be clear like I've never used Harvey right.

I've grown to appreciate the complexity and of the AI native agentic systems with connections and managing context and memory and other capabilities that don't come for free and they don't come in the model, not yet.
there's a million choices and it's really hard to tell the difference between them
at the end of the day all of them should be judged by their utility

kp.k: Copilot criticism rests on anecdote and an unverified mechanism
kp.d: Theodoropoulos reports poorer results from Microsoft Copilot than general models in his comparisons, illustrating this with a basketball-champions query approximately 90 days earlier. He speculates that token throttling to manage consumption explains the shorter response, while expressly acknowledging uncertainty. This is a host's product criticism based on a non-legal example, not a controlled evaluation of legal capability.
qs: I I ran a sidebyside maybe 90 days ago where I said give me all of the NCAA basketball men's uh champions.
Copilot, because I believe they're token throttling, gave me the last 20 years and only the name of the winner.
I really don't know for sure but I think they're token throttling to manage consumption.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The panel presents AI NDA review as useful first-pass assistance, with workflow automation and reusable playbooks extending its utility, but not as dependable final legal work. It also predicts displacement, changing software economics and wider use of multiple models.
pts.d: Rob Saccone says Claude Co-work's substantive NDA findings were similar to those of ordinary Claude chat in the demonstrated example; its added value was a cleaner process, document access, multi-step execution and formatted deliverables. He argues that written playbooks can scale individual expertise. Josh Kubicki characterises the plugin as a capable junior issue-spotter rather than a substitute for contextual legal judgment: it identified inappropriate provisions but missed indemnification nuance. Saccone's experiment also suggests that skill wording and model choice affect results, while Kubicki reports variation even with the same input. Kubicki predicts lawyers and legal-business professionals will work with multiple models and increasingly evaluate and update their own skills. Saccone independently predicts displacement, pointing to inexpensive model experiments compared with lawyers' hourly rates. Separately, Ted Theodoropoulos endorses an explanation he encountered in an unnamed X analysis: agents could reduce employee numbers and thereby demand for per-seat software. That mechanism originates in the quoted analysis, not in independent evidence produced by the host. Saccone argues that purpose-built legal-AI products can add context, memory, integrations and workflow capabilities beyond a raw model; his comments about Harvey are explicitly not based on having used it. The panel also warns that local Co-work files are not equivalent to local-only inference: document contents reach Anthropic's backend, so confidentiality depends on applicable terms rather than the desktop interface or sandbox.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a fabricated NDA demonstration, Saccone's exploratory model-and-skill evaluation, Kubicki's repeated trials and practitioner experience. Market-size and displacement claims are estimates or predictions, not measured market outcomes.
pts.d: Saccone used an intentionally one-sided agreement labelled as a mutual NDA. His Skill Check application compared publicly available NDA skills, a law-firm checklist and a minimal prompt across models. Scoring used his own simple rubric for planted issues and an LLM-as-judge approach, rather than independent human legal grading. He acknowledges that he is not a lawyer and invites scrutiny of the rubric. He reports that prompt-only ranked second among skills, describes a 69%–87% score spread for Gemini 3 Pro across instructions, and says concrete checklists worked better than verbosity in that comparison. These are task-specific exploratory results, not a general legal-accuracy benchmark. Kubicki reports at least ten fresh-session runs of the same NDA and prompt, with variable outputs. His legal review found consistent flagging of non-solicitation, but failure to distinguish negligence from gross negligence in indemnification, with differing treatment across outputs. Saccone estimates 15–20 million NDAs and assumes only 20–25% receive review, grounding the thought exercise in US employer-business counts and common NDA uses; no external dataset is supplied. He reports roughly 50–60 experiments costing two dollars and contrasts that with $500–$1,000 hourly legal rates, without establishing equivalent final legal services or including verification costs. Theodoropoulos offers his company's negotiation experience as context for selective outside-counsel use, not as a measured AI effect. His Copilot criticism rests on personal comparisons, including a basketball-history query about 90 days earlier; token throttling is expressly his conjecture. Saccone's enterprise-product observations draw on industry experience, but he disclaims direct Harvey experience. His description of large firms routing model use through Microsoft contracts is likewise experiential.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current capabilities are described at the time of the 2026 panel; Kubicki gives a 12–18-month horizon for wider evaluation practices, while displacement and per-seat business-model pressure have no firm deadline.
pts.d: The NDA demonstration and comparisons concern then-current products, with Saccone noting that he added Gemini 3.1 Pro immediately after its release. Kubicki expects local LLMs 'shortly' and predicts that the skill/model evaluation practices demonstrated will become relevant to many people within 12–18 months of the panel. This is a forecast, not a documented adoption trend. Saccone's displacement claim is directional and undated. The per-seat scenario is conditional on agents replacing substantial employee work; Theodoropoulos also anticipates business adjustments rather than treating software-company failure as inevitable. For NDA review, Kubicki explicitly rejects using the unmodified plugin to eliminate further review. Results depend on client and transaction context, organisational standards, skill wording, model choice and run-to-run variability. He qualifies criticism by noting that human lawyers can miss issues too. Saccone treats multi-model judging and judging the judges as possible extensions, not established production safeguards, and argues for open rubrics and testability. Confidentiality claims are conditional on the product's data handling and contractual terms: the speakers do not establish the precise retention or privilege implications of Co-work's access to local context files.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include businesspeople signing NDAs, small companies buying legal advice, lawyers and legal-business professionals, high-volume institutional users, legal-AI vendors, law-firm software buyers and per-seat software businesses.
pts.d: Saccone frames NDA triage around a small software startup receiving a larger prospective partner's agreement and highlights agreements signed without legal review as the potential market. This concerns business contracting risk and unmet review demand, rather than a demonstrated civil access-to-justice outcome. Theodoropoulos describes Infodash handling familiar, minor licensing changes internally while escalating unusual or substantive issues to outside counsel; this illustrates a buyer's existing cost-and-speed trade-off. Kubicki points to a research university handling hundreds of NDAs monthly and illustrates customisation for a professional-services agency concerned about IP transfers. Lawyers remain responsible for contextual interpretation and checking AI work, while lawyers and legal-business professionals are forecast to take on skill creation, updating and model evaluation. Saccone sees law-firm buyers facing difficulty distinguishing numerous AI products and advocates judging their utility. Legal-AI vendors can differentiate through enterprise capabilities, whereas per-seat software suppliers face the conditional revenue risk described in the X analysis endorsed by Theodoropoulos. Firms and individuals handling privileged or confidential materials face data-governance risks even when files appear to remain on their own machines; Saccone says large firms often use Microsoft-hosted models under enterprise contracts.
